script.opening: "Hi — sorry, it's me again. I've got another water infection, I just know the feeling now, burning and weeing constantly. It's my fourth this year. Can you just put another course of antibiotics through? I don't need to come in, I know what it is. I just want to nip it before the weekend. Same as last time is fine."

facts.text: If asked: started yesterday — burning when passing urine, going every half hour, urgency. A bit of lower tummy ache. No visible blood in the urine.
No fever or shivers, no pain in the back or sides, no vomiting. Not pregnant (you have the coil). No vaginal discharge.

facts.topic: The pattern — only if asked when they tend to happen
facts.text: "Honestly? They always seem to start a day or two after we've... you know. Been together." You feel embarrassed saying it.
Periods are getting irregular. Hot flushes now and again. Vaginal dryness for about a year, making sex uncomfortable — you have not mentioned it to anyone.
"Not great — coffee mostly, maybe one glass of water." You hold on at work because you are busy.
Three this year, all treated by phone with nitrofurantoin; each cleared. Previous urine tests grew E. coli. Never had a kidney infection.
Hormonal coil (Mirena). No other medicines. No allergies. No diabetes. No history of kidney stones.
The dryness and pain during sex are affecting your relationship and you feel embarrassed. Say this only if the doctor asks gently and without judgement.

Apologetic and in a hurry — you want a prescription. If the doctor asks about sex in a matter-of-fact, kind way, answer honestly. If they suggest a plan to stop these infections (urine test, a cream for the dryness, a tablet after sex), you are pleasantly surprised: "I didn't know you could do that."

ice.ideas: "It's another water infection — I know the feeling."
ice.concerns: Embarrassment, and feeling like a nuisance for ringing again.
ice.expectations: "Same antibiotics as last time." You would welcome something to stop them coming back, once you trust the doctor.

cues: "It's my fourth this year." — say in the opening.
"They always seem to come after... well." — say hesitantly if asked about a pattern.
"Things have been a bit uncomfortable down there lately." — say if asked about the menopause or dryness.

checkpoints.text: Treats the acute episode appropriately but recognises RECURRENT UTI (≥3/year) as the real issue needing a proper review — not endless reflex phone scripts — and ideally confirms with a URINE CULTURE to guide therapy and exclude resistance/relapse
Explores and addresses the CONTRIBUTORS: the post-coital pattern, peri-menopausal vaginal ATROPHY/dryness, and low fluid intake — rather than just prescribing

Offers TOPICAL VAGINAL OESTROGEN having identified the atrophy — for her vaginal dryness (urogenital atrophy, NICE NG23), while being accurate that NICE NG112 recommends it for recurrent-UTI prevention in POSTmenopausal women, so in a perimenopausal woman any reduction in UTIs is a possible extra benefit rather than the NG112 indication — a key, often-missed intervention

Works through the PROPHYLAXIS LADDER: self-care (hydration, post-coital voiding, not delaying voiding), a single antibiotic dose after sex (NICE NG112), then methenamine hippurate or continuous antibiotic prophylaxis if needed — with review at 6 months; not a self-start/standby course, which is not an NG112 prevention option; may discuss non-antibiotic options (e.g. D-mannose) and antimicrobial-stewardship

Considers when to investigate/refer (haematuria, persistent infection despite treatment, atypical organisms, suspected structural cause, recurrent in men) and screens red flags (fever, loin pain, haematuria — pyelonephritis)

Surfaces the embarrassment about the post-coital link and menopausal dryness gently and non-judgementally, de-shaming it, so the real (treatable) contributors can be addressed rather than colluding with "don’t make it a thing"
Frames the review and vaginal oestrogen as the route OUT of the infection cycle (and helpful for her sex life), engaging her rather than just refilling antibiotics

Safety-nets and follows up: urine culture, the prophylaxis plan and vaginal oestrogen, pyelonephritis red flags (fever/loin pain/vomiting → urgent), a review to assess the plan, and stewardship — ending the reflex-script cycle

worked.txt: "I’ll help you with this flare — but four in a year tells me we should do more than keep firing antibiotics at it, because that just breeds resistance and never fixes WHY it keeps coming back. Let me sort today, ideally with a urine sample to be sure which bug, and then let’s actually break the cycle."

"Can I ask a couple of things — no embarrassment, this is really common: do you notice they often come on after sex? … And being around the menopause, any vaginal dryness or soreness? … Thank you for telling me. Those two things are huge clues, and the good news is they’re very treatable — it’s not just bad luck."

"Here’s something that can really help with the dryness: a low-dose oestrogen cream or pessary used in the vagina. Around the menopause the tissues thin and dry, which also makes infections more likely. It’s a proven treatment for the dryness and for comfort during sex, and after the menopause it’s one of the recommended ways to cut repeat UTIs — for you now, any drop in infections would be a welcome bonus. It’s a tiny dose, used locally, and very safe."

"Alongside that: drink more through the day, wee after sex, don’t hold on when you need to go. If those aren’t enough, we can give you a single antibiotic to take after sex, or, if that isn’t enough, a non-antibiotic tablet called methenamine or a low daily antibiotic dose for a while, reviewed at six months — a proper plan, stepped up only as needed."

"And honestly — the link with sex is nothing to be embarrassed about, it’s just anatomy and incredibly common. I’d much rather you could tell me than suffer four infections a year in silence. Sorting this should mean fewer infections AND a better, more comfortable sex life."

"So: I’ll treat today with a culture, start you on the vaginal oestrogen, and set up the prevention plan, then review how it’s going. If you ever get a fever, loin/back pain, vomiting, or blood in your urine — that’s a kidney infection, contact us urgently. You rang for another quick course; what I’d like to give you is a way to stop needing them."

f.learning: Recurrent UTI in a woman (≥3/year) is the real issue — not a reflex phone-script opportunity — and warrants a proper review (ideally a urine culture to guide therapy and exclude resistance/relapse) rather than endless empirical courses that drive resistance and miss treatable contributors. Explore and address the contributors: the post-coital pattern, peri-menopausal vaginal ATROPHY/dryness, and low fluid intake. A key, often-missed intervention is TOPICAL VAGINAL OESTROGEN: NICE NG112 recommends considering it for recurrent UTI in POSTmenopausal women, and in a perimenopausal woman like Carla it treats the dryness/dyspareunia of urogenital atrophy (NICE NG23), with any reduction in UTIs a possible bonus. Work the prophylaxis LADDER — self-care (hydration, post-coital voiding), a single antibiotic dose after sex, then methenamine hippurate or continuous prophylaxis if needed (standby self-start courses are not an NG112 prevention option), with review and stewardship — and know when to investigate/refer (haematuria, treatment failure, atypical organisms, structural concern, men). The examinable hidden agenda is embarrassment about the sexual link and menopausal dryness driving "just give me antibiotics, don’t make it a thing"; surface and de-shame it gently, frame vaginal oestrogen and the ladder as the route OUT of the cycle (and better for her sex life), and safety-net pyelonephritis.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG112 — Urinary tract infection (recurrent): antimicrobial prescribing (2018, updated 2024)
knowledge.summary: Three UTIs in a year is recurrent UTI. Treat today’s episode with a culture, then work the NICE NG112 ladder: self-care, vaginal oestrogen where menopausal atrophy is present, a single antibiotic dose after a clear trigger such as sex, then methenamine or daily prophylaxis with review.

points.t: Recurrent UTI = 2 or more in 6 months, or 3 or more in 12 months (NICE NG112). Send a urine culture before antibiotics in recurrent UTI and use previous sensitivities. For a non-pregnant woman, NICE NG109 first choices are nitrofurantoin 100 mg modified-release twice daily for 3 days (if eGFR ≥45) or trimethoprim 200 mg twice daily for 3 days if resistance risk is low.

Explain triggers and offer self-care advice: drinking enough to keep urine pale, not delaying voiding, passing urine after sex, avoiding constipation. Cranberry and D-mannose may be discussed as the woman’s choice, with honest mention that evidence is limited or uncertain (NICE NG112).

NICE NG112 advises considering vaginal oestrogen for postmenopausal women with recurrent UTI when self-care alone is not enough, reviewed within 12 months. Oral HRT does not reduce UTIs. For a peri-menopausal woman with vaginal dryness, vaginal oestrogen is also a treatment for urogenital atrophy in its own right (NICE NG23, updated April 2026).

Where there is a clear trigger such as intercourse, NICE NG112 supports a single antibiotic dose taken after exposure — e.g. trimethoprim 200 mg, or nitrofurantoin (dose per BNF) — chosen by previous culture results. Review the benefit within 6 months.

If the earlier rungs fail: methenamine hippurate as an alternative to daily antibiotics (NICE NG112, 2024 update), or daily trimethoprim 100 mg or nitrofurantoin 50–100 mg at night. Review at 6 months. Nitrofurantoin can rarely cause lung and liver reactions — stop if pulmonary symptoms develop (MHRA Drug Safety Update, April 2023).

NICE NG112: refer men, anyone with recurrent upper UTI, and recurrent lower UTI where the cause is unknown; seek advice in pregnancy. Visible haematuria that is not explained by UTI, or persists after treatment, follows. Fever, loin pain or vomiting suggests pyelonephritis (NICE NG111).

Impact on her relationship and sex life, low fluid intake, and the wish to keep it quick.
Urine culture before antibiotics; face-to-face review for vaginal examination with a chaperone offered.
Post-coital pattern and peri-menopausal atrophy as contributors; STI, vaginal cause and pregnancy considered.
Screened for pyelonephritis (fever, loin pain, vomiting) and visible haematuria; knows NG112 referral groups.
Named recurrent UTI (≥3 in 12 months) with post-coital and atrophic contributors.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

Addressed dryness and dyspareunia as a problem in its own right, plus hydration and voiding habits.
Face-to-face review booked; pyelonephritis symptoms named; plan if not better after the course; prophylaxis reviewed at 6 months.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (same old infection); concern (it will keep happening and is affecting home life); expectation (a quick script by phone).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

model.text: Hello, is that Carla Mendez? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Before we go on, can you confirm your date of birth for me, and are you somewhere you can talk privately?
model.why: Identity and privacy checks on a telephone consultation

model.text: Yes, I’m at home on my own. Sorry, it’s me again — it’s another water infection. Burning, weeing all the time. Fourth one this year. Can you just put the same antibiotics through? I want it sorted before the weekend.

No need to apologise — this sounds miserable, and I’ll make sure you’re treated today. Can I ask a few quick questions to make sure it is the usual thing, and then, if you’re willing, spend a couple of minutes on why it keeps coming back?
model.why: Acknowledges her request and agrees a shared agenda early

model.text: Okay. I don’t really want to make it a whole thing, though.
Understood — I’ll keep it focused. Any fever or shivers, pain in your back or sides, feeling sick or being sick?
model.why: Screens for pyelonephritis before a remote prescription

model.text: No, none of that. Just the burning and going all the time.
Any blood in the urine, any unusual vaginal discharge, and is there any chance you could be pregnant?
model.why: Excludes haematuria, an STI or vaginal cause, and pregnancy

model.text: No blood, no discharge. And no, I’m not pregnant.
Thank you. The last ones grew a germ called E. coli on the lab test. When did this one start, and how are you drinking through the day?
model.why: Uses previous culture results and asks about fluid intake

model.text: Yesterday. And honestly I don’t drink much — a couple of coffees, that’s it.
That helps. Can I ask something that many women find a bit awkward, but it’s one of the most useful questions I can ask? Do you notice the infections tend to start a day or two after sex?
model.why: Normalises a sensitive question before asking it

model.text: …Yes. Pretty much every time. I didn’t want to say.

Thank you for telling me — it’s really common and simply down to anatomy, nothing you’re doing wrong. And being in your forties, have you noticed any changes in your periods, or any vaginal dryness or soreness?
model.why: Explores peri-menopausal atrophy as a treatable contributor

model.text: My periods have been all over the place. And yes, dryness — sex has been uncomfortable. That’s partly why I didn’t want to get into it. It’s embarrassing.
It isn’t embarrassing to me at all, and I’m glad you said it. What worries you most about all this?
model.why: Responds to the embarrassment cue and invites her concerns

model.text: That it’s going to keep happening. And that it’s affecting things at home. I just thought if I kept it quick nobody would ask.

That makes complete sense. Here’s how I see it: with four in a year, this counts as recurrent infection, so we should treat today AND look at why. You’ve given me two big clues — the link with sex, and the dryness. Around the menopause the vaginal tissue thins and gets drier, and that makes infections more likely.
model.why: Names recurrent UTI and links it to the contributors she disclosed

model.text: So it’s not just bad luck?

Not just bad luck — and that’s good news, because both are treatable. For today, I’ll prescribe a three-day course, chosen using your last lab results. I’d also like a urine sample dropped in before you start, so the lab can check this germ is still sensitive. Is that doable today?
model.why: Treats the acute episode per NG109 with a culture for stewardship

model.text: Yes, I can drop it in this afternoon.

Then there are steps to stop the cycle. First, simple things: drinking enough that your urine stays pale, not holding on, and passing urine soon after sex. Second — and this is the one often missed — a low-dose oestrogen cream or pessary used in the vagina. It helps the dryness and discomfort, and in women past the menopause it clearly reduces these infections. It’s a small local dose. How would you feel about that?
model.why: Works the NG112 ladder, including vaginal oestrogen, honestly framed

model.text: I didn’t know that was a thing. If it helps the dryness too… yes, I’d try it.

Good. If infections still follow sex after that, the next option is a single antibiotic tablet taken after sex, rather than full courses. And if that’s not enough, there are daily options we’d review every six months. We step up only if we need to.
model.why: Shares options as a staged plan she can choose into

model.text: That sounds better than ringing every few months.

Exactly. I’d like to see you in person in the next couple of weeks, once this infection has settled, to look at the dryness properly and start the oestrogen. A chaperone is always available if you’d like one. Would that be okay?
model.why: Converts a reflex script into a planned review, offering a chaperone

model.text: Yes. I’d rather do it properly now, to be honest.

Please ring us the same day, or 111 out of hours, if you get a temperature, shivers, pain in your back or side, vomiting, or blood in your urine — that can mean the infection has reached the kidney. And if you’re no better after the course, let us know so we can check the lab result.
model.why: Specific pyelonephritis safety-net and a treatment-failure plan

model.text: Okay, I’ll watch for that.
Just so I know I’ve explained it clearly — can you tell me what the plan is from here?
Sample in today, three days of tablets, drink more and wee after sex, then come in to talk about the cream.
Perfect. Thank you for being open with me today — it’s what lets us actually fix this. Anything else you wanted to ask?
model.why: Affirms her disclosure and shares the floor

model.text: No, that’s it. Thanks — I feel a lot less stupid about it now.

social.t: Painful sex and repeated infections after intercourse affect relationships and self-esteem. Embarrassment keeps women from mentioning it; asking sensitively is part of the treatment.
Wanting it “sorted before the weekend” reflects practical pressure. A plan that cuts future infections saves her more time than repeated calls.

legal.t: GMC guidance on remote prescribing (Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices, 2021) expects an adequate assessment and access to the records before prescribing — a repeat script without assessment does not meet it.

professional.t: Culture-guided treatment and a structured NICE NG112 plan protect her and the wider population from resistance. Document the rationale for each course.
Offer a chaperone for vaginal examination and record the offer and her decision (GMC, Intimate examinations and chaperones, 2024).

community.t: The NHS Pharmacy First uncomplicated-UTI pathway excludes women with recurrent UTI, so her care stays with the practice; pharmacists can still support self-care advice.
The British Menopause Society and NHS menopause information can help her understand genitourinary symptoms and treatment options.

redFlags: Fever, rigors, loin pain, nausea or vomiting — possible pyelonephritis (NICE NG111), not a routine repeat script
Visible haematuria not explained by UTI or persisting after treatment — pathway
Pregnancy, abnormal discharge or genital ulcers — change the diagnosis and the drug choice
psychosocial: Embarrassment about the link with sex and about vaginal dryness
Impact on her relationship and comfort during sex
Time pressure and the wish to avoid coming in
ice: Idea: “It’s the same infection, same antibiotics will fix it”
Concern: it will keep happening and is affecting things at home — too embarrassing to say
Expectation: a quick phone prescription without “making it a thing”

playbook.diagnosis: “Four infections in a year is what we call recurrent urine infection. The link with sex and the dryness around the menopause are both making infections more likely — and both can be treated.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the vaginal lining as the bladder’s front-line defence. Around the menopause that lining gets thinner and drier, so germs get through more easily — especially after sex. Topping up oestrogen locally rebuilds the defence.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted this kept quick, and I understand why — it’s not an easy thing to talk about. I’m really glad you told me, because it means we can stop this happening rather than just treating each one.”
management.psychosocial: Normalise the post-coital pattern and the dryness; offer vaginal oestrogen as help for comfort during sex as well as infections; keep the plan practical around her time.
sharedPlan: Urine culture today; three-day course per NICE NG109 guided by previous sensitivities
Self-care (fluids, voiding after sex, not delaying) and vaginal oestrogen (NICE NG112 / NG23), reviewed within 12 months
If still recurring: post-coital single dose, then methenamine or daily prophylaxis with 6-monthly review
safetyNet: Fever, loin pain, vomiting or blood in urine — same-day contact or 111
Not better after the course — call for the culture result; face-to-face review in 2 weeks

pitfalls.intro: This station is not about antibiotic doses. It is failed by either rubber-stamping the fourth script or refusing it with a lecture, and by never reaching the two treatable contributors she is too embarrassed to raise.

items.fail: Issuing “the same as last time” after a one-line history.
items.why: No red-flag screen, no culture and no recognition of recurrent UTI: “management not in line with current UK best practice” (NICE NG109 / NG112).
items.fix: Screen for kidney infection, send a culture, choose the drug by previous sensitivities, and name recurrent UTI out loud.

items.fail: Refusing to prescribe until she comes in, and explaining antimicrobial resistance at length.
items.why: She has a symptomatic infection today. Withholding treatment to force a review reads as punitive and loses her trust.
items.fix: Treat today and invite the review as the route out: “Let’s sort this one, then stop the next.”

items.fail: Never asking about sex or vaginal dryness.
items.why: The post-coital pattern and atrophy are the treatable causes; missing them leaves only more antibiotics.
items.fix: Normalise first, then ask: “Many women notice these start after sex — have you?” and “Any dryness or soreness?”

items.fail: Jumping straight to daily antibiotic prophylaxis.
items.why: NICE NG112 orders the ladder: self-care, vaginal oestrogen, single-dose after a trigger, then methenamine or daily prophylaxis.
items.fix: Offer the steps in order and explain you step up only if needed, with review at 6 months.

items.fail: Hearing “it’s embarrassing” and moving on to the next question.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s cues.” Her embarrassment is the hidden agenda of the case.
items.fix: Pause and de-shame: “It isn’t embarrassing to me, and I’m glad you said it — it helps me help you.”

items.fail: Closing with “come back if it doesn’t get better”.
items.why: Vague safety-netting on a remote prescription is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Name fever, loin pain, vomiting and blood in the urine; say who to call and when; book the face-to-face review.

items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “Dryness around the menopause”, “a single tablet after sex”, “a cream used in the vagina”.

Pyelonephritis screen, haematuria, discharge, pregnancy, previous cultures, fluids. Then gently ask about sex and vaginal dryness.
“Four in a year is recurrent infection — and you’ve given me two treatable clues.”
Culture plus three-day course. Self-care, vaginal oestrogen, post-coital single dose, then methenamine or daily prophylaxis only if needed. Book a face-to-face review.
Kidney-infection symptoms named, plan if not better, teach-back, thank her for being open.

wordPics.fail: Issues another course with no questions, or refuses outright and lectures on resistance; no pyelonephritis screen; never asks about sex or dryness; no culture; no follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Screens red flags, treats with a suitable three-day course and a culture, recognises recurrent UTI, gives self-care advice and mentions prophylaxis options and a review.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: asks about sex and dryness in a way that visibly relaxes her; offers vaginal oestrogen with an honest explanation; lays out the NG112 ladder as her choice; books a face-to-face review with a chaperone offer; she ends the call relieved rather than judged.

avoid.dont: “I can’t keep giving you antibiotics — you’re going to become resistant.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll treat you today — and I’d like to help you stop needing these courses at all.”
avoid.why: Stewardship delivered as a scolding loses her; stewardship delivered as a better plan wins both domains.

SCA_MODELS.why: Names recurrent UTI and links it to the contributors she disclosed

SCA_MODELS.text: So it’s not just bad luck?

Not just bad luck — and that’s good news, because both are treatable. For today, I’ll prescribe a three-day course, chosen using your last lab results. I’d also like a urine sample dropped in before you start, so the lab can check this germ is still sensitive. Is that doable today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Treats the acute episode per NG109 with a culture for stewardship

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, I can drop it in this afternoon.

Then there are steps to stop the cycle. First, simple things: drinking enough that your urine stays pale, not holding on, and passing urine soon after sex. Second — and this is the one often missed — a low-dose oestrogen cream or pessary used in the vagina. It helps the dryness and discomfort, and in women past the menopause it clearly reduces these infections. It’s a small local dose. How would you feel about that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Works the NG112 ladder, including vaginal oestrogen, honestly framed

SCA_MODELS.text: I didn’t know that was a thing. If it helps the dryness too… yes, I’d try it.

Good. If infections still follow sex after that, the next option is a single antibiotic tablet taken after sex, rather than full courses. And if that’s not enough, there are daily options we’d review every six months. We step up only if we need to.
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares options as a staged plan she can choose into

SCA_MODELS.text: That sounds better than ringing every few months.

Exactly. I’d like to see you in person in the next couple of weeks, once this infection has settled, to look at the dryness properly and start the oestrogen. A chaperone is always available if you’d like one. Would that be okay?
SCA_MODELS.why: Converts a reflex script into a planned review, offering a chaperone

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. I’d rather do it properly now, to be honest.

Please ring us the same day, or 111 out of hours, if you get a temperature, shivers, pain in your back or side, vomiting, or blood in your urine — that can mean the infection has reached the kidney. And if you’re no better after the course, let us know so we can check the lab result.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific pyelonephritis safety-net and a treatment-failure plan

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay, I’ll watch for that.
Just so I know I’ve explained it clearly — can you tell me what the plan is from here?
Sample in today, three days of tablets, drink more and wee after sex, then come in to talk about the cream.
Perfect. Thank you for being open with me today — it’s what lets us actually fix this. Anything else you wanted to ask?
SCA_MODELS.why: Affirms her disclosure and shares the floor

SCA_MODELS.text: No, that’s it. Thanks — I feel a lot less stupid about it now.

SCA_STEM.name: Carla Mendez
pmh: Recurrent lower urinary tract infection — three treated episodes earlier this year
meds: Three acute antibiotic courses for UTI this year
SCA_STEM.recent: Three UTI episodes this year, each treated with a short antibiotic course. Previous cultures grew E. coli. No recurrent-UTI review on record.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone request for another course of antibiotics: “fourth water infection this year”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG112 — Urinary tract infection (recurrent): antimicrobial prescribing (2018, updated 2024)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Three UTIs in a year is recurrent UTI. Treat today’s episode with a culture, then work the NICE NG112 ladder: self-care, vaginal oestrogen where menopausal atrophy is present, a single antibiotic dose after a clear trigger such as sex, then methenamine or daily prophylaxis with review.

points.t: Recurrent UTI = 2 or more in 6 months, or 3 or more in 12 months (NICE NG112). Send a urine culture before antibiotics in recurrent UTI and use previous sensitivities. For a non-pregnant woman, NICE NG109 first choices are nitrofurantoin 100 mg modified-release twice daily for 3 days (if eGFR ≥45) or trimethoprim 200 mg twice daily for 3 days if resistance risk is low.

Explain triggers and offer self-care advice: drinking enough to keep urine pale, not delaying voiding, passing urine after sex, avoiding constipation. Cranberry and D-mannose may be discussed as the woman’s choice, with honest mention that evidence is limited or uncertain (NICE NG112).

NICE NG112 advises considering vaginal oestrogen for postmenopausal women with recurrent UTI when self-care alone is not enough, reviewed within 12 months. Oral HRT does not reduce UTIs. For a peri-menopausal woman with vaginal dryness, vaginal oestrogen is also a treatment for urogenital atrophy in its own right (NICE NG23, updated April 2026).

Where there is a clear trigger such as intercourse, NICE NG112 supports a single antibiotic dose taken after exposure — e.g. trimethoprim 200 mg, or nitrofurantoin (dose per BNF) — chosen by previous culture results. Review the benefit within 6 months.

If the earlier rungs fail: methenamine hippurate as an alternative to daily antibiotics (NICE NG112, 2024 update), or daily trimethoprim 100 mg or nitrofurantoin 50–100 mg at night. Review at 6 months. Nitrofurantoin can rarely cause lung and liver reactions — stop if pulmonary symptoms develop (MHRA Drug Safety Update, April 2023).

NICE NG112: refer men, anyone with recurrent upper UTI, and recurrent lower UTI where the cause is unknown; seek advice in pregnancy. Visible haematuria that is not explained by UTI, or persists after treatment, follows. Fever, loin pain or vomiting suggests pyelonephritis (NICE NG111).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Acknowledged the request without refusing or rubber-stamping it; agreed to treat and to explore why it keeps recurring.
Impact on her relationship and sex life, low fluid intake, and the wish to keep it quick.
Picked up “don’t make it a whole thing” and her hesitation, and asked sensitively about sex and dryness.
Idea (same old infection); concern (it will keep happening and is affecting home life); expectation (a quick script by phone).
Urine culture before antibiotics; face-to-face review for vaginal examination with a chaperone offered.
Post-coital pattern and peri-menopausal atrophy as contributors; STI, vaginal cause and pregnancy considered.
Screened for pyelonephritis (fever, loin pain, vomiting) and visible haematuria; knows NG112 referral groups.
Named recurrent UTI (≥3 in 12 months) with post-coital and atrophic contributors.
Three-day course per NG109 guided by prior culture; NG112 ladder — self-care, vaginal oestrogen, post-coital single dose, then methenamine or daily prophylaxis.
Addressed dryness and dyspareunia as a problem in its own right, plus hydration and voiding habits.
Face-to-face review booked; pyelonephritis symptoms named; plan if not better after the course; prophylaxis reviewed at 6 months.

social.t: Painful sex and repeated infections after intercourse affect relationships and self-esteem. Embarrassment keeps women from mentioning it; asking sensitively is part of the treatment.
Wanting it “sorted before the weekend” reflects practical pressure. A plan that cuts future infections saves her more time than repeated calls.

legal.t: GMC guidance on remote prescribing (Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices, 2021) expects an adequate assessment and access to the records before prescribing — a repeat script without assessment does not meet it.

professional.t: Culture-guided treatment and a structured NICE NG112 plan protect her and the wider population from resistance. Document the rationale for each course.
Offer a chaperone for vaginal examination and record the offer and her decision (GMC, Intimate examinations and chaperones, 2024).

community.t: The NHS Pharmacy First uncomplicated-UTI pathway excludes women with recurrent UTI, so her care stays with the practice; pharmacists can still support self-care advice.
The British Menopause Society and NHS menopause information can help her understand genitourinary symptoms and treatment options.

redFlags: Fever, rigors, loin pain, nausea or vomiting — possible pyelonephritis (NICE NG111), not a routine repeat script
Visible haematuria not explained by UTI or persisting after treatment — pathway
Pregnancy, abnormal discharge or genital ulcers — change the diagnosis and the drug choice
psychosocial: Embarrassment about the link with sex and about vaginal dryness
Impact on her relationship and comfort during sex
Time pressure and the wish to avoid coming in
ice: Idea: “It’s the same infection, same antibiotics will fix it”
Concern: it will keep happening and is affecting things at home — too embarrassing to say
Expectation: a quick phone prescription without “making it a thing”

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Four infections in a year is what we call recurrent urine infection. The link with sex and the dryness around the menopause are both making infections more likely — and both can be treated.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the vaginal lining as the bladder’s front-line defence. Around the menopause that lining gets thinner and drier, so germs get through more easily — especially after sex. Topping up oestrogen locally rebuilds the defence.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted this kept quick, and I understand why — it’s not an easy thing to talk about. I’m really glad you told me, because it means we can stop this happening rather than just treating each one.”
management.psychosocial: Normalise the post-coital pattern and the dryness; offer vaginal oestrogen as help for comfort during sex as well as infections; keep the plan practical around her time.
sharedPlan: Urine culture today; three-day course per NICE NG109 guided by previous sensitivities
Self-care (fluids, voiding after sex, not delaying) and vaginal oestrogen (NICE NG112 / NG23), reviewed within 12 months
If still recurring: post-coital single dose, then methenamine or daily prophylaxis with 6-monthly review
safetyNet: Fever, loin pain, vomiting or blood in urine — same-day contact or 111
Not better after the course — call for the culture result; face-to-face review in 2 weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is not about antibiotic doses. It is failed by either rubber-stamping the fourth script or refusing it with a lecture, and by never reaching the two treatable contributors she is too embarrassed to raise.

items.fail: Issuing “the same as last time” after a one-line history.
items.why: No red-flag screen, no culture and no recognition of recurrent UTI: “management not in line with current UK best practice” (NICE NG109 / NG112).
items.fix: Screen for kidney infection, send a culture, choose the drug by previous sensitivities, and name recurrent UTI out loud.

items.fail: Refusing to prescribe until she comes in, and explaining antimicrobial resistance at length.
items.why: She has a symptomatic infection today. Withholding treatment to force a review reads as punitive and loses her trust.
items.fix: Treat today and invite the review as the route out: “Let’s sort this one, then stop the next.”

items.fail: Never asking about sex or vaginal dryness.
items.why: The post-coital pattern and atrophy are the treatable causes; missing them leaves only more antibiotics.
items.fix: Normalise first, then ask: “Many women notice these start after sex — have you?” and “Any dryness or soreness?”

items.fail: Jumping straight to daily antibiotic prophylaxis.
items.why: NICE NG112 orders the ladder: self-care, vaginal oestrogen, single-dose after a trigger, then methenamine or daily prophylaxis.
items.fix: Offer the steps in order and explain you step up only if needed, with review at 6 months.

items.fail: Hearing “it’s embarrassing” and moving on to the next question.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s cues.” Her embarrassment is the hidden agenda of the case.
items.fix: Pause and de-shame: “It isn’t embarrassing to me, and I’m glad you said it — it helps me help you.”

items.fail: Closing with “come back if it doesn’t get better”.
items.why: Vague safety-netting on a remote prescription is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Name fever, loin pain, vomiting and blood in the urine; say who to call and when; book the face-to-face review.

items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “Dryness around the menopause”, “a single tablet after sex”, “a cream used in the vagina”.
